# Skill Sheet: CT Abdomen Pelvis with Contrast — Acute Diverticulitis (Query)

## Scan Context
- **Modality:** CT with IV contrast; enteral contrast (oral/rectal) per dictation
- **Primary region:** Abdomen and pelvis
- **Imaged volume:** Diaphragmatic dome to ischial symphysis
- **In-scope:** Liver, gallbladder, biliary tree (gross), pancreas, spleen, kidneys, ureters, adrenal glands, aorta and major abdominal vessels, mesenteric vessels, small bowel, colon (all segments, with emphasis on sigmoid and rectum), appendix, omentum, peritoneum, retroperitoneum, bladder, uterus, ovaries, pelvic bones, abdominal wall, inguinal regions
- **Secondary visible regions:**
  - Lung bases (lower lobes) → "The visualised lung bases are clear."
  - Distal thoracic aorta → "The distal thoracic aorta is unremarkable."
  - Lumbar and sacral vertebral bodies → "No osseous abnormality is identified in the visualised spine."
- **Out of scope:**
  - Biliary tree microarchitecture (requires MRCP)
  - Small bowel mucosal detail (ulceration, early ischaemic mucosal change) (requires MR enterography)
  - Lung parenchymal detail (requires CT chest)
- **Contrast:** IV contrast stated in scan type; enteral contrast per dictation
- **Modality non-assessables:**
  - Biliary ductal mucosal detail not resolvable below standard CT spatial resolution — requires MRCP
  - Small bowel mucosal ulceration and early ischaemic change below standard CT resolution thresholds — requires MR enterography
  - Adrenal microadenomas <1 cm below reliable detection on standard abdominal CT protocol

## Clinical Lane
- **Question:** Confirm or exclude acute sigmoid diverticulitis and, if confirmed, determine complication severity (abscess, perforation, fistula, obstruction) to gate management pathway — antibiotics alone versus percutaneous drainage versus surgical intervention
- **Purpose:** Diagnostic / triage
- **Primary hypothesis:** Acute sigmoid diverticulitis
- **Differentials in scope:**
  - **Triage:** Acute diverticulitis (confirm or exclude) versus alternative aetiologies of left iliac fossa pain (colorectal malignancy, epiploic appendagitis, ovarian pathology, ureteric calculus, ischaemic colitis, abscess of other origin)
  - **Aetiology (if diverticulitis confirmed — complication severity):**
    - Uncomplicated (Hinchey I) — pericolic fat stranding, diverticula at inflamed segment, no collection, no extraluminal air
    - Pericolic/paracolic abscess (Hinchey II) — walled-off rim-enhancing fluid collection adjacent to inflamed segment, ± internal air-fluid level
    - Generalised peritonitis (Hinchey III) — free peritoneal fluid of mixed attenuation, extraluminal air beyond pericolic region, diffuse mesenteric and peritoneal stranding
    - Distant abscess (Hinchey II variant) — rim-enhancing collection in pelvis, subhepatic space, or other non-adjacent location
    - Stricture / partial obstruction — luminal narrowing at inflamed segment with proximal colonic dilatation
    - Fistula — abnormal enhancing tract from inflamed segment to bladder, vagina, adjacent bowel loop, or abdominal wall
  - **Alternative diagnoses to exclude (if diverticulitis not confirmed):**
    - Colorectal malignancy — eccentric or concentric wall thickening >1 cm, luminal narrowing, heterogeneous enhancement, mesorectal or mesenteric lymphadenopathy
    - Epiploic appendagitis — oval fat-density lesion with hyperdense rim adjacent to colonic serosa
    - Ovarian pathology (postmenopausal) — adnexal mass, complex free fluid
    - Ureteric calculus — hyperdense focus in ureter with proximal hydroureter
    - Ischaemic colitis — segmental wall thickening in a watershed distribution, thumbprinting, mesenteric vessel involvement
- **Clinical history modifiers:**
  - 66F, postmenopausal → colorectal malignancy must be actively excluded on imaging even if diverticulitis is confirmed; ovarian pathology less common but not excluded → management implication: if diverticulitis confirmed, colonoscopy at 6–8 weeks is mandatory to exclude underlying malignancy; if a mass is seen, MDT referral
  - 4 days of symptoms → subacute window; early pericolic abscess formation is within the expected timeframe; epiploic appendagitis less likely (typically self-limiting <72 h) → management implication: if abscess >3 cm identified, urgent interventional radiology referral for drainage; if <3 cm, antibiotics may suffice with interval imaging
  - Fever 38.2, WCC 15, CRP 180 → systemic inflammatory response; CRP >150 elevates the pre-test probability of complicated diverticulitis (abscess, perforation) over uncomplicated disease → management implication: high threshold to search for and report even small collections or subtle extraluminal air; if no complication identified on imaging, the impression should note the discordance and recommend clinical follow-up
  - Referring clinician's working diagnosis of diverticulitis → imaging must confirm or exclude; if excluded, an alternative aetiology must be identified or the report must state no explanation found → management implication: the impression must directly answer "diverticulitis yes/no" before addressing any subsidiary findings

## Structural Pattern
- **Sections:** COMPARISON, TECHNIQUE, FINDINGS, IMPRESSION (LIMITATIONS included only if a genuine protocol or study-specific degradation meaningfully precludes a clinical expectation)
- **P1 belongs:** Inflamed sigmoid segment (location, extent, wall thickness, mural enhancement, diverticula), pericolic fat stranding, pericolic/paracolic abscess, extraluminal air (pericolic or free), fistula, stricture with proximal colonic dilatation, reactive mesenteric lymphadenopathy, reactive peritoneal thickening, free peritoneal fluid attributable to the diverticulitis
- **P1 does NOT belong:** Residual abdominal and pelvic anatomy (liver, gallbladder, pancreas, spleen, kidneys, ureters, adrenals, aorta, mesenteric vessels, small bowel, remaining colon, bladder, uterus, ovaries, bones, soft tissues, lung bases)
- **Primary system (priority-ordered):** Inflamed sigmoid segment first (location, extent, wall thickness, enhancement, diverticula) → pericolic fat stranding → complications in descending severity: extraluminal air → abscess (location, size, rim enhancement) → fistula → stricture/obstruction → reactive lymphadenopathy → proximal colonic dilatation
- **Sweep order:** Sigmoid and rectum (implied region from left iliac fossa pain) → remaining colon → small bowel → liver, gallbladder, biliary tree, pancreas, spleen → kidneys, ureters, adrenals → aorta and mesenteric vessels → omentum, peritoneum, retroperitoneum → bladder, uterus, ovaries → bones, soft tissues, inguinal regions → secondary visible regions (lung bases, distal thoracic aorta, visualised spine)
- **Macro-structure:** FLAT
- **Normal-study path:** "The sigmoid and rectum are unremarkable, with no wall thickening, pericolic fat stranding, or extraluminal air. The remaining colon and small bowel are normal in wall thickness and calibre, with no dilatation, obstruction, or abnormal enhancement. The liver is normal in size, shape, and attenuation, with no focal lesion or biliary dilatation. The gallbladder is normal in size with no wall thickening or pericholecystic fluid. The pancreas is normal in size and attenuation with no peripancreatic stranding. The spleen is normal in size. The kidneys are normal in size and enhancement, with no hydronephrosis or calculus. The ureters are not dilated. The adrenal glands are unremarkable. The aorta and mesenteric vessels are patent with no aneurysm or thrombus. The omentum and peritoneum are unremarkable, with no free fluid or ascites. The bladder is normal in size and wall thickness. The uterus and ovaries are normal in size and morphology. The retroperitoneum is clear. The visualised lung bases are clear. No osseous abnormality is identified. No soft-tissue abnormality is identified."

## Companion Matrix
- **In-scope companions:**
  - Inflamed sigmoid segment — location (specific diverticula, extent in cm), wall thickness (mm), mural enhancement pattern (circumferential vs eccentric), presence of diverticula
  - Pericolic fat stranding — extent (cm), distribution (pericolic vs extending into mesentery or paracolic gutter)
  - Pericolic/paracolic abscess — location relative to inflamed segment, largest dimension (cm) or volume by ABC/2 if irregular, rim enhancement, internal air-fluid level
  - Extraluminal air — location (pericolic vs free in peritoneum), volume (small vs large), associated free fluid
  - Fistula — tract location, target organ (bladder, vagina, small bowel, abdominal wall), enhancing wall
  - Stricture / obstruction — luminal calibre at stricture (mm), proximal colonic dilatation (max diameter in cm), level of transition
  - Reactive mesenteric lymphadenopathy — location, short-axis size (mm), number
  - Proximal colonic dilatation — maximum luminal diameter (cm), level of transition
  - Free peritoneal fluid — volume (small / moderate / large), distribution, attenuation (simple vs complex/mixed)
  - Reactive peritoneal thickening — location, thickness (mm)
- **Mandatory negatives:**
  - "No mass lesion or asymmetric wall thickening to suggest colorectal malignancy."
  - "No hyperdense focus within the ureter or perinephric space to suggest obstructing calculus."
  - "No adnexal mass or complex free fluid to suggest ovarian pathology."
  - "No segmental colonic wall thickening or thumbprinting in a distribution separate from the sigmoid to suggest ischaemic colitis."
  - "No oval fat-density lesion with hyperdense rim adjacent to the colonic serosa to suggest epiploic appendagitis."
  - "No extraluminal air beyond the pericolic region to suggest generalised perforation."
- **Out-of-scope suppressed:**
  - Biliary tree microarchitecture (requires MRCP)
  - Small bowel mucosal detail (requires MR enterography)
  - Lung parenchymal detail (requires CT chest)

## Style Exemplars

- **Sigmoid diverticulitis (uncomplicated):** "The sigmoid colon shows focal circumferential wall thickening to 8 mm over a 4 cm segment at the sigmoid–descending junction, with surrounding pericolic fat stranding extending 3 cm. Several diverticula are visible at the affected segment. No pericolic abscess, extraluminal air, or fistula is identified."

- **Pericolic abscess:** "A 3.2 cm rim-enhancing fluid collection is seen posterior to the inflamed sigmoid segment, with a small internal air-fluid level, consistent with a pericolic abscess."

- **Colorectal mass (alternative diagnosis):** "The rectosigmoid junction shows a 3.4 cm eccentric, irregular wall thickening with luminal narrowing to 8 mm and heterogeneous enhancement, with three enlarged mesorectal lymph nodes (largest 14 mm short axis)."

- **Free perforation:** "Extraluminal air tracks along the left paracolic gutter with moderate-volume free peritoneal fluid of mixed attenuation, consistent with free perforation."

## Terminology Rules
- **Preferred:** "pericolic fat stranding" (not "fat streaking" or "fat stranding" alone — "pericolic" localises to the relevant compartment)
- **Preferred:** "wall thickening" (not "wall oedema" — CT demonstrates thickness, not oedema per se)
- **Preferred:** "rim-enhancing collection" (not "ring-enhancing" — rim is the standard CT descriptor)
- **Preferred:** "extraluminal air" when localised to the pericolic region; "free air" reserved for generalised peritoneal air
- **Findings-only vs Impression-permitted:** "Hinchey" — reserve for impression synthesis; findings describe the imaging features (collection size, air, fluid, stranding) without assigning a Hinchey grade unless dictated

## Conditional Suppression Rules
- IF the sigmoid diverticulitis is named with its descriptor in P1, the subsequent colon sweep names the remaining colon only, without restating the sigmoid finding
- IF a triage differential (malignancy, calculus, ovarian pathology, ischaemic colitis, epiploic appendagitis) is excluded by the imaging, state it as a single compact negative in FINDINGS and carry it into the IMPRESSION as a direct negative answer; do not elaborate in both locations
- IF dictation is silent about an in-scope structure the sweep order visits, render the structure's canonical default-normal line at its sweep position; if dictation specifies a positive finding, replace the canonical line; if dictation flags a technical limitation, that triggers LIMITATIONS inclusion
- IF a dictated positive finding implicates a structure as a companion (e.g. pericolic stranding implicating the adjacent peritoneum), the canonical default-normal line for that structure is dropped or rendered in contingent form; coverage remains obligatory, the specific normal assertion does not
- IF multiple negatives fire in one subsystem (e.g. no calculus, no hydronephrosis, no renal mass), consolidate into a single sentence
- IF a descriptor is mentioned once in P1, it is not repeated in the sweep or impression
- Adjacent-in-sweep structures whose canonical lines are all normal consolidate into a single paragraph; a paragraph earns its own boundary only when it carries a positive finding, a differential-targeted negative the clinical question turns on, or a clinical pivot between body regions
- Gender is established as female (66F); canonical pelvic lines name the uterus and ovaries directly

## Measurement Conventions
- **Abscess:** largest dimension in cm (or volume by ABC/2 if irregular); location relative to inflamed segment; >3 cm is the threshold at which percutaneous drainage is typically indicated
- **Wall thickening:** maximum thickness in mm; extent in cm; >1 cm with eccentricity raises malignancy concern
- **Colonic dilatation:** maximum luminal diameter in cm; level of transition named anatomically

## Impression Exemplars

- **Opening convention:** Confirmed diverticulitis (with complication tier) opens the impression; if diverticulitis is excluded, the negative answer to the primary question opens, followed by any alternative aetiology identified; on a broad screen with no single pathology, the most actionable finding opens
- **Normal exemplar:** "No acute diverticulitis identified. The sigmoid and rectum are unremarkable. No mass lesion, obstructing calculus, adnexal abnormality, ischaemic colitis, or free peritoneal fluid identified. No alternative aetiology identified on this study."
- **Abnormal exemplar:** "Acute sigmoid diverticulitis, uncomplicated. No pericolic abscess, free perforation, or fistula identified. Gastroenterology referral recommended for colonoscopy at 6–8 weeks to exclude underlying malignancy."
- **Complicated exemplar:** "1. Acute sigmoid diverticulitis with a 3.4 cm pericolic abscess posterior to the inflamed segment. Urgent interventional radiology and colorectal surgery referrals recommended. 2. No evidence of free perforation or fistula. 3. No alternative pathology identified."
- **Descriptor propagation:** Complication severity tier (uncomplicated vs abscess vs perforation vs fistula) propagates — it gates the management pathway. Abscess size >3 cm propagates — it triggers the drainage referral. Free perforation propagates — it escalates to emergency surgical referral. Malignancy features (eccentric thickening >1 cm, mesorectal nodes) propagate — they gate oncology MDT referral. Diagnostic-criterion descriptors (wall thickness 8 mm, 4 cm extent, pericolic stranding) do NOT propagate — the diagnosis name encodes them.
- **Recommendation scope:**
  - IMAGING: CT chest if pulmonary pathology is implicated by clinical correlation; MR enterography if small bowel pathology is suspected and not excluded on CT
  - REFERRAL: Colorectal surgery (urgent for abscess >3 cm or perforation; routine for uncomplicated diverticulitis); Interventional radiology (urgent, for abscess >3 cm); Gastroenterology (routine, for post-acute colonoscopy at 6–8 weeks)
  - MDT: Colorectal MDT (for complicated diverticulitis with stricture or fistula, or if malignancy cannot be excluded on imaging)
  - TISSUE: Image-guided biopsy of pericolic mass if malignancy cannot be excluded on imaging
  - CORRELATION: Clinical correlation if imaging is negative but inflammatory markers remain elevated; colonoscopy at 6–8 weeks post-acute episode to exclude underlying malignancy
- **Guideline hooks:** Hinchey classification (diverticulitis severity); NICE diverticular disease management guidance; BSG (British Society of Gastroenterology) guidelines for post-diverticulitis colonoscopy

# Skill Sheet: MRI Brain with Contrast — Intracranial Metastatic Disease in Known Breast Cancer

## Scan Context
- **Modality:** MRI brain with intravenous gadolinium contrast (T1 pre- and post-contrast, T2, FLAIR, DWI/ADC, T2* or SWI)
- **Primary region:** Intracranial (brain parenchyma, meninges, ventricular system, skull base)
- **Imaged volume:** Vertex to skull base, including orbits at the inferior margin and upper cervical spinal canal (C1–C2) at the caudal margin
- **In-scope:** Cerebral hemispheres (cortex, subcortical white matter, grey-white junction), basal ganglia, thalami, brainstem, cerebellum, ventricular system, meninges (dura, arachnoid, pia), intracranial dural venous sinuses, skull base, orbits (partial)
- **Secondary visible regions:**
  - Orbits → "The orbits are unremarkable."
  - Visualised paranasal sinuses → "The visualised paranasal sinuses are clear."
  - Upper cervical spinal canal (C1–C2) → "The upper cervical spinal canal is unremarkable."
- **Out of scope:**
  - Systemic metastatic disease (requires CT chest/abdomen/pelvis or PET-CT)
  - Spinal cord and cauda equina (requires whole-spine MRI with contrast)
  - Carotid and vertebral artery lumen (requires CTA or dedicated MRA)
- **Contrast:** Gadolinium-enhanced (stated in scan-type name)
- **Modality non-assessables:**
  - Vascular lumen detail (stenosis, dissection, aneurysm morphology) — standard brain MRI does not include time-of-flight or contrast-enhanced MRA; requires dedicated CTA or MRA
  - Calvarial cortical bone architecture (lytic vs sclerotic destruction) — MRI demonstrates marrow replacement but cannot resolve cortical destruction; CT head superior
  - Spinal cord below C2 — outside imaged volume; requires whole-spine MRI

## Clinical Lane
- **Question:** Rule in or rule out intracranial metastatic disease (or alternative intracranial pathology) to determine whether the headaches, confusion, and vomiting are attributable to a treatable intracranial process, and to gate neurosurgical and oncological management
- **Purpose:** Diagnostic / triage
- **Primary hypothesis:** Intracranial metastatic disease (ER+ breast cancer)
- **Differentials in scope:**
  - **Triage:** Intracranial mass lesion(s) vs leptomeningeal disease vs haemorrhage vs acute ischaemia vs venous sinus thrombosis vs no intracranial pathology
  - **Aetiology (if enhancing mass/lesion confirmed):**
    - Metastatic deposit — enhancing lesion(s) at grey-white junction, well-defined margins, variable size, surrounding vasogenic oedema; multiple lesions strongly favour metastatic
    - High-grade glioma — solitary irregular enhancing mass with central necrosis, heterogeneous enhancement, infiltrative margins
    - Primary CNS lymphoma — homogeneously enhancing periventricular mass, may be multifocal, minimal surrounding oedema relative to size
    - Pyogenic abscess — ring-enhancing lesion with central restricted diffusion on DWI, surrounding vasogenic oedema
    - Haemorrhagic metastasis — enhancing lesion with mixed T1/T2 signal indicating blood products within or adjacent to the mass
  - **Aetiology (if leptomeningeal enhancement confirmed):**
    - Leptomeningeal carcinomatosis — nodular or linear leptomeningeal enhancement, multifocal, may involve cranial nerves, associated parenchymal deposits
    - Inflammatory or infectious meningitis — diffuse smooth leptomeningeal enhancement, basilar predominance (fungal/TB), associated ventriculitis
  - **Aetiology (if haemorrhage confirmed):**
    - Haemorrhagic metastasis — haemorrhage within or immediately adjacent to an enhancing lesion
    - Primary intracerebral haemorrhage — non-enhancing haemorrhagic collection without adjacent mass
    - CVST with haemorrhagic infarction — haemorrhage in a venous distribution with dural sinus filling defect
  - **Imaging-silent aetiologies:**
    - Coagulopathy *(imaging-silent — requires clinical/laboratory correlation)*
    - Letrozole-related adverse effect *(imaging-silent — requires clinical/laboratory correlation)*
- **Clinical history modifiers:**
  - Known ER+ breast cancer → high prior for intracranial metastatic disease (breast is the second most common primary for brain metastases); if metastatic disease confirmed, oncological MDT pathway activates and treatment planning (surgery, stereotactic radiosurgery, whole-brain radiotherapy, systemic therapy adjustment) is gated by the imaging findings
  - On letrozole (aromatase inhibitor) → confirms active endocrine therapy; progression on therapy may alter systemic treatment pathway and raises prior for treatment-resistant disease if metastatic deposits are identified
  - Two weeks of headaches → subacute timeline favours progressive mass effect or growing lesion over hyperacute event; raises prior for metastatic deposit with vasogenic oedema rather than haemorrhage or large-vessel occlusion
  - Acute confusion → suggests raised ICP or diffuse cortical involvement; raises the urgency threshold for neurosurgical referral if mass effect or hydrocephalus is identified
  - Vomiting → correlate of raised ICP; combined with confusion and headache the triad raises prior for significant mass effect or obstructive hydrocephalus; if midline shift exceeds 5 mm or hydrocephalus is present, neurosurgical referral is urgent

## Structural Pattern
- **Sections:** COMPARISON, TECHNIQUE, FINDINGS, IMPRESSION
- **P1 belongs:** Primary intracranial pathology (metastatic deposit(s), primary neoplasm, abscess, haemorrhage) plus all causally linked companions: surrounding vasogenic oedema, mass effect (midline shift, herniation), obstructive hydrocephalus, leptomeningeal or dural involvement as part of the same process, venous sinus thrombosis if causally related
- **P1 does NOT belong:** Unrelated incidental findings (small-vessel ischaemic change, incidental pituitary microadenoma, incidental cervical disc protrusion)
- **Primary system (priority-ordered):** Mass/lesion first (location, number, size, enhancement pattern), then associated oedema and mass effect (midline shift in mm, direction, herniation), then hydrocephalus (communicating vs obstructive, ventricular width), then leptomeningeal/dural involvement if part of the same process, then venous sinus assessment
- **Sweep order:** Systematic (no lateralised symptom): cerebral hemispheres (grey-white junction, cortex, subcortical white matter, deep grey nuclei) → ventricles and periventricular region → brainstem and cerebellum → meninges (dura, leptomeninges) → dural venous sinuses → skull base and orbits → upper cervical spinal canal
- **Macro-structure:** FLAT
- **Normal-study path:** "The cerebral hemispheres, basal ganglia, thalami, brainstem, and cerebellum show no abnormal signal intensity, restricted diffusion, or enhancement. The grey-white junction is clear bilaterally. The ventricles are normal in size and configuration with no periventricular oedema. The sulci and cisterns are of normal calibre with no leptomeningeal or dural enhancement. The dural venous sinuses are patent. The orbits and visualised paranasal sinuses are unremarkable. The upper cervical spinal canal is unremarkable."

## Companion Matrix
- **In-scope companions:**
  - Vasogenic oedema — extent in cm from lesion margin, lobes involved, T2/FLAIR hyperintensity
  - Mass effect — midline shift in mm at the level of the septum pellucidum, direction; subfalcine, uncal, or transtentorial herniation (qualitative)
  - Hydrocephalus — communicating vs obstructive, lateral ventricle width in mm at the foramen of Monro, periventricular oedema
  - Leptomeningeal disease — linear vs nodular enhancement, distribution (sulci, cisterns, cranial nerves, periventricular)
  - Dural involvement — dural-based enhancement, dural tail, pachymeningeal thickening (mm)
  - Venous sinus thrombosis — filling defect in transverse, sigmoid, or superior sagittal sinus on post-contrast T1
  - Number and distribution of lesions — count, bilateral vs unilateral, grey-white junction vs cortical vs deep vs cerebellar
- **Mandatory negatives:**
  - "No restricted diffusion on DWI to suggest acute ischaemic infarction."
  - "No ring-enhancing lesion with central diffusion restriction to suggest pyogenic abscess."
  - "No diffuse leptomeningeal enhancement to suggest meningitis or leptomeningeal carcinomatosis."
  - "No abnormal T1 or T2* signal to suggest intracranial haemorrhage."
  - "The dural venous sinuses are patent with no filling defect."
  - "No periventricular homogeneously enhancing mass to suggest primary CNS lymphoma."
- **Out-of-scope suppressed:**
  - Systemic metastatic disease (requires CT chest/abdomen/pelvis or PET-CT)
  - Spinal metastatic disease (requires whole-spine MRI with contrast)
  - Carotid/vertebral artery stenosis or dissection (requires CTA or MRA)

## Style Exemplars

- **Metastatic deposit (solitary, grey-white junction):**
  "A 2.3 cm enhancing lesion is present at the left frontoparietal grey-white junction with 3 cm of surrounding vasogenic oedema extending into the adjacent white matter."

- **Multiple metastatic deposits:**
  "Three enhancing lesions are identified: a 1.8 cm deposit at the right frontal grey-white junction, a 0.9 cm deposit in the left parietal lobe, and a 0.5 cm deposit in the right cerebellar hemisphere, each with a rim of surrounding vasogenic oedema."

- **Leptomeningeal carcinomatosis:**
  "Nodular leptomeningeal enhancement is present along the left frontal and temporal sulci and within the left lateral ventricle, with associated thickening of the left optic nerve sheath."

- **Mass effect with midline shift:**
  "The left-sided mass effect produces 8 mm of rightward midline shift at the level of the septum pellucidum, with effacement of the left lateral ventricle and early subfalcine herniation."

## Terminology Rules
- **Preferred:** "vasogenic oedema" (specifies the mechanism and distinguishes from cytotoxic oedema; "brain swelling" or "perilesional oedema" are imprecise)
- **Preferred:** "grey-white junction" (standard radiological term; "cortical-subcortical junction" is non-standard)
- **Preferred:** "leptomeningeal" (specifies arachnoid and pia; "meningeal" alone is ambiguous and may imply pachymeningeal)
- **Preferred:** "metastatic deposit" / "cerebral metastases" (diagnostic term for the impression; "brain tumour" or "brain lesion" are non-specific and belong in findings only)
- **Suppressed:** "avidly enhancing" → "enhancing" (avoid subjective intensity qualifiers unless truly distinguishing from a hypoenhancing lesion)
- **Findings-only vs Impression-permitted:** "metastatic deposit" — reserve for impression synthesis when the imaging pattern supports the attribution; findings describe the imaging features (enhancing lesion, location, size, oedema, number) without the diagnostic label

## Conditional Suppression Rules
- IF the index finding is named with its descriptor in P1 (e.g. "left frontoparietal metastatic deposit, 2.3 cm") THEN the sweep paragraph for that region names the structure only ("the left frontal lobe is otherwise unremarkable") without restating the descriptor
- IF a triage differential is excluded by the imaging (e.g. no restricted diffusion excludes acute ischaemia) THEN state it as a single compact negative in FINDINGS and carry it into the IMPRESSION as a direct negative answer; do not elaborate in both locations
- IF dictation is silent about an in-scope structure the sweep order visits THEN render the structure's canonical default-normal line at its sweep position; if dictation specifies a positive finding, replace the canonical line; if dictation flags a technical limitation, that triggers LIMITATIONS inclusion
- IF a dictated positive implicates a structure as a companion (e.g. a left frontal mass with vasogenic oedema extending into the left temporal lobe) THEN the canonical normal line for the left temporal lobe is dropped or rendered in contingent form ("the left temporal lobe is unremarkable apart from the oedema described above") rather than asserting normality
- IF multiple negatives fire in one subsystem (e.g. no haemorrhage, no ischaemia, no mass in the right hemisphere) THEN consolidate into a single sentence: "The right cerebral hemisphere shows no abnormal signal, enhancement, or restricted diffusion."
- A descriptor mentioned once is not repeated in subsequent paragraphs; structures are described in one place
- Adjacent-in-sweep structures whose canonical lines are all normal consolidate into a single paragraph (e.g. orbits + paranasal sinuses + upper cervical canal in one terminal sentence); a paragraph earns its own boundary only when it carries a positive finding, a differential-targeted negative the clinical question turns on, or a clinical pivot between compartments

## Measurement Conventions
- **Metastatic deposit size:** maximum diameter in mm (or cm if ≥10 mm) — required for each lesion; relevant to surgical resectability and stereotactic radiosurgery planning
- **Midline shift:** mm at the level of the septum pellucidum — required when ≥5 mm; gates neurosurgical urgency
- **Ventricular width:** lateral ventricle width in mm at the foramen of Monro — required when hydrocephalus is suspected or present

## Impression Exemplars

- **Opening convention:** Index finding when any intracranial pathology is confirmed; negative answer only when every question is answered negatively; the most actionable finding on a broad screen
- **Normal exemplar:** "No intracranial metastatic disease, primary neoplasm, or acute ischaemic or haemorrhagic pathology identified. No leptomeningeal or dural enhancement. No mass effect or hydrocephalus. The dural venous sinuses are patent. No restricted diffusion. No intracranial abnormality identified."
- **Abnormal exemplar:** "Multiple intracranial metastatic deposits with 8 mm rightward midline shift. Neurosurgical referral urgent. Oncological MDT review recommended."
- **Complicated exemplar:** "Multiple intracranial metastatic deposits with 12 mm rightward midline shift and early uncal herniation. Leptomeningeal carcinomatosis involving the left frontal and temporal sulci. Obstructive hydrocephalus, lateral ventricle width 38 mm. Neurosurgical referral urgent. Oncological MDT review recommended."
- **Descriptor propagation:** Midline shift >5 mm (escalates urgency to neurosurgical referral); number of deposits (single vs multiple changes surgical vs radiosurgical pathway); herniation (escalates to emergency); hydrocephalus with ventricular measurement (gates CSF diversion urgency); leptomeningeal involvement (separate management pathway). Individual deposit size, oedema extent, and enhancement pattern are diagnostic-criterion descriptors and do NOT propagate — the diagnosis name encodes them
- **Recommendation scope:**
  - IMAGING: Whole-spine MRI with contrast to assess for spinal metastatic disease (when intracranial metastases confirmed)
  - IMAGING: CT chest/abdomen/pelvis or PET-CT for systemic staging (when metastatic disease confirmed)
  - REFERRAL: Neurosurgical referral (urgent when midline shift >5 mm or herniation; routine when small asymptomatic deposits)
  - MDT: Oncological MDT (breast cancer) for treatment planning (when metastatic disease confirmed and acute management stabilised)
  - CORRELATION: Clinical correlation for symptoms not explained by imaging (when study is negative)
- **Guideline hooks:** NICE guideline for management of brain metastases; Royal College of Radiologists reporting standards for intracranial metastatic disease. No specific RADS classification system applies to intracranial metastases.

# Skill Sheet: MRI Whole Spine with Contrast — Query Malignant Spinal Cord Compression

## Scan Context
- **Modality:** MRI with intravenous gadolinium contrast; T1-weighted, T2-weighted, STIR (or T2 fat-saturated), and post-contrast T1-weighted fat-saturated sequences
- **Primary region:** Whole spine (cervical, thoracic, lumbar, sacral)
- **Imaged volume:** Skull base (foramen magnum) to sacrococcygeal junction
- **In-scope:** Vertebral bodies (all levels), posterior elements, spinal canal, thecal sac, spinal cord (cervical, thoracic, conus medullaris), cauda equina, paravertebral and prevertebral soft tissues, epidural space, intervertebral discs, facet joints, neural foramina, sacrum, coccyx
- **Secondary visible regions:**
  - Lung bases (thoracic sequences) → "Lung bases are unremarkable within the imaged volume."
  - Upper abdominal organs (lumbar sequences) → "Upper abdominal organs are unremarkable within the imaged volume."
  - Pelvic viscera (sacral sequences) → "Pelvic viscera are unremarkable within the imaged volume."
- **Out of scope:** Full lung parenchyma (lung bases visible on thoracic sequences; full lung requires CT chest); pelvic organ detail including prostate and pelvic lymph nodes (requires dedicated pelvic MRI); brain parenchyma (requires dedicated brain MRI)
- **Contrast:** Intravenous gadolinium-enhanced (stated in scan type)
- **Modality non-assessables:** Cortical bone detail and subtle cortical breach — MRI demonstrates marrow oedema and destruction but cortical integrity is better assessed on CT (requires CT spine); calcification detail — MRI does not depict calcification, so osteoblastic (sclerotic) metastases may be undercharacterised (requires CT); small epidural collections <3 mm — below resolution threshold on standard whole-spine sequences (requires thin-slice dedicated imaging)

## Clinical Lane
- **Question:** Rule in or out malignant spinal cord compression (MSCC) to gate urgent neurosurgical decompression or emergent radiotherapy within hours of confirmation
- **Purpose:** Acute triage / diagnostic
- **Primary hypothesis:** Malignant spinal cord compression secondary to metastatic prostate carcinoma
- **Differentials in scope:**
  - **Triage:** Malignant spinal cord compression (MSCC) vs other causes of thecal sac or cord compression (epidural haemorrhage, infection, degenerative stenosis, disc herniation, primary spinal neoplasm)
  - **Aetiology (if compression confirmed):**
    - Metastatic disease — vertebral body marrow replacement (T1 hypointense, T2 variable), epidural extension through posterior cortical breach, paravertebral soft tissue mass, enhancing on post-contrast T1, multiple levels
    - Epidural haemorrhage — T1/T2 signal of blood products (age-dependent), no enhancing soft tissue mass, no vertebral body marrow replacement
    - Infection (discitis, osteomyelitis, epidural abscess) — disc space involvement, paravertebral or prevertebral enhancement, rim-enhancing collection, adjacent vertebral body marrow oedema
    - Degenerative stenosis — disc bulging or protrusion, ligamentum flavum hypertrophy, facet arthropathy, no enhancing mass, no marrow replacement
    - Primary spinal neoplasm — intradural or extradural mass, different enhancement pattern, typically single level
- **Clinical history modifiers:**
  - Known metastatic prostate cancer with PSA 85 → overwhelmingly increases prior for MSCC; the imaging question is confirmatory (level, extent, mechanism) rather than diagnostic; the impression must convey urgency of intervention within hours of confirmation
  - Three weeks progressive thoracic back pain → localises the primary site to the thoracic spine; the sweep leads with thoracic levels; progressive nature indicates a growing epidural or paravertebral component that will not resolve spontaneously
  - 48 hours bilateral leg weakness with two falls → indicates significant cord compression with established myelopathy; this is a neurosurgical emergency; the impression must convey extreme urgency and the window for intervention is measured in hours, not days
  - New urinary hesitancy → suggests conus medullaris or cauda equina involvement, or severe thoracic cord compression with autonomic dysfunction; elevates urgency to emergency; the conus and cauda equina must be specifically assessed and reported

## Structural Pattern
- **Sections:** COMPARISON, TECHNIQUE, FINDINGS, IMPRESSION
- **P1 belongs:** The compressive lesion (vertebral body metastasis, epidural extension, paravertebral mass), degree of thecal sac and cord compression, cord signal change (myelopathy) at the level of compression, additional vertebral body metastases (skip metastases), additional paravertebral or epidural disease, conus and cauda equina involvement if present, additional sites of disease visible in the imaged volume
- **P1 does NOT belong:** Residual normal anatomy at unaffected levels, secondary visible regions (lung bases, upper abdominal organs, pelvic viscera) unless they show disease, degenerative changes unrelated to the compressive pathology
- **Primary system (priority-ordered):** The compressive lesion and its mechanism (retropulsed bone, epidural soft tissue, paravertebral mass) first; degree of thecal sac and cord compression second; cord signal change (myelopathy) third; additional vertebral body metastases fourth; additional paravertebral or epidural disease fifth; conus and cauda equina assessment sixth; additional sites of disease in the imaged volume seventh
- **Sweep order:** The compressive pathology (P1) leads regardless of level. The remaining sweep proceeds cranio-caudal: cervical spine, thoracic spine (above and below the compressive level), lumbar spine, sacrum and coccyx, paravertebral and prevertebral soft tissues (all levels), conus and cauda equina, secondary visible regions (lung bases, upper abdominal organs, pelvic viscera), residual bones and soft tissues
- **Macro-structure:** FLAT
- **Normal-study path:** "No evidence of spinal cord compression or thecal sac compromise at any level. The cervical, thoracic, lumbar, and sacral vertebral bodies show normal marrow signal with no focal replacement, collapse, or oedema. The posterior elements, intervertebral discs, and neural foramina are unremarkable throughout. No paravertebral, prevertebral, or epidural soft tissue abnormality. The spinal canal is patent at all levels. The conus medullaris terminates at the expected level with no signal abnormality. The cauda equina is unremarkable. Lung bases, upper abdominal organs, and pelvic viscera are unremarkable within the imaged volume."

## Companion Matrix
- **In-scope companions:**
  - Vertebral body metastasis — level(s), number of levels involved, degree of collapse (percentage or mm), marrow signal (T1 hypointensity, T2 variable), enhancement pattern on post-contrast T1, cortical breach (posterior, lateral, anterior)
  - Epidural extension — level(s), extent (circumferential, anterior, posterior, lateral), degree of thecal sac compression (partial, near-complete, complete), AP diameter of thecal sac in mm at the level of maximum compression
  - Paravertebral soft tissue mass — level(s), craniocaudal extent in cm, AP diameter in cm, relationship to neural foramina, prevertebral vs paravertebral vs retrocrural
  - Cord signal change — T2 hyperintensity at the level of compression, craniocaudal extent in mm or levels, indicating myelopathy
  - Conus medullaris — level of termination, signal, any compression or signal abnormality
  - Cauda equina — any compression, signal abnormality, enhancement
  - Additional vertebral body metastases — levels, number, degree of collapse, marrow signal
  - Additional paravertebral or epidural disease — levels, extent, relationship to neural foramina
  - Sacral and coccygeal involvement — if within imaged volume
  - Additional sites of disease in the imaged volume (paraspinal, retroperitoneal, pelvic)
- **Mandatory negatives:**
  - "No epidural haemorrhage identified." (excludes epidural haemorrhage as cause of compression)
  - "No disc space abnormality, paravertebral collection, or rim-enhancing fluid to suggest discitis, osteomyelitis, or epidural abscess." (excludes infection)
  - "No intradural mass or leptomeningeal enhancement identified." (excludes primary spinal neoplasm or leptomeningeal disease)
  - "No degenerative disc disease, ligamentum flavum hypertrophy, or facet arthropathy causing thecal sac compromise at any level." (excludes degenerative stenosis as cause of compression)
  - "The conus medullaris and cauda equina are unremarkable." (excludes conus or cauda equina pathology relevant to urinary symptoms)
  - "No additional paravertebral or epidural soft tissue abnormality at levels other than the primary compressive lesion." (excludes skip metastases or additional disease burden)
- **Out-of-scope suppressed:** Full lung parenchyma (requires CT chest); pelvic organ detail including prostate and pelvic lymph nodes (requires dedicated pelvic MRI); brain parenchyma (requires dedicated brain MRI)

## Style Exemplars

- **Vertebral body metastasis with epidural extension:**
  "T7 vertebral body shows marrow replacement with T1 hypointensity and post-contrast enhancement, with 40% collapse and posterior cortical breach. An epidural soft tissue mass extends from T6 to T8, compressing the thecal sac to 4 mm anteroposteriorly with near-complete cord compression."

- **Cord signal change (myelopathy):**
  "The thoracic cord at T7 shows T2 hyperintensity extending from T6 to T8, consistent with myelopathy at the level of compression."

- **Paravertebral soft tissue mass:**
  "A paravertebral soft tissue mass at T7 measures 3.2 cm craniocaudally, extending into the left neural foramen and displacing the descending aorta laterally."

- **Additional vertebral body metastases:**
  "Additional vertebral body metastases are identified at T3, T9, L1, and L4, each showing T1 hypointensity and post-contrast enhancement without significant collapse."

## Terminology Rules
- **Preferred:** "Malignant spinal cord compression" (MSCC) — preferred over "spinal cord compression" when the aetiology is malignant; "spinal cord compression" alone is non-specific and does not convey the oncological urgency
- **Preferred:** "Thecal sac compression" — preferred over "spinal canal stenosis" when the compression is from an extrinsic soft tissue or bony mass rather than degenerative change
- **Preferred:** "Marrow replacement" — preferred over "marrow oedema" when the signal abnormality represents tumour infiltration; "marrow oedema" implies a reversible or inflammatory process
- **Preferred:** "Retropulsed bone" — preferred over "bone fragment" for posterior cortical breach with retropulsion into the spinal canal
- **Findings-only vs Impression-permitted:** "MSCC" — reserve for impression synthesis; findings describe the imaging features (epidural extension, thecal sac compression, cord signal change) without naming the diagnosis

## Conditional Suppression Rules
- IF the compressive lesion is named with its level and descriptor in P1, THEN the sweep paragraph for that vertebral level names the structure only, without restating the descriptor
- IF a triage differential is excluded by the imaging, THEN state it as a single compact negative in FINDINGS and carry it into the IMPRESSION as a direct negative answer; do not elaborate in both locations
- IF dictation is silent about an in-scope structure the sweep order visits, THEN render the structure's canonical default-normal line at its sweep position; silence is not omission — it is the default rendering
- IF multiple negatives fire in one subsystem (e.g. no disc disease, no ligamentum flavum hypertrophy, no facet arthropathy), THEN consolidate into a single sentence
- IF a descriptor is mentioned once in P1, THEN it is not repeated in subsequent paragraphs; structures are described in one place
- IF adjacent-in-sweep structures are all normal, THEN consolidate into a single paragraph; a paragraph earns its own boundary only when it carries case-specific content (a positive finding, a differential-targeted negative, or a clinical pivot between body regions)
- IF the clinical history establishes male gender (72M, prostate cancer), THEN pelvic structures use gender-appropriate naming if dictation names them; otherwise the generic line "pelvic viscera are unremarkable within the imaged volume" applies

## Measurement Conventions
- **Thecal sac / cord compression:** Anteroposterior diameter in mm at the level of maximum compression; degree stated as partial, near-complete, or complete
- **Vertebral body collapse:** Percentage of original vertebral body height (or mm loss); required when collapse is present
- **Paravertebral / epidural soft tissue:** Craniocaudal extent in cm and anteroposterior diameter in cm; required when a mass is present

## Impression Exemplars

- **Opening convention:** MSCC confirmed → opens with the diagnosis, level, severity, and complication; MSCC excluded → opens with the negative answer; broad screen → opens with the most actionable finding
- **Normal exemplar:** "No evidence of malignant spinal cord compression. No vertebral body marrow replacement, epidural or paravertebral soft tissue abnormality, or thecal sac compromise at any level. No epidural haemorrhage, infection, or intradural mass identified. The conus medullaris and cauda equina are unremarkable."
- **Abnormal exemplar:** "Malignant spinal cord compression at T7 with near-complete thecal sac compromise and cord myelopathy. Additional vertebral body metastases at T3, T9, L1, and L4. Urgent neurosurgical referral recommended."
- **Complicated exemplar:** "Malignant spinal cord compression at T7 with complete thecal sac compromise and cord myelopathy. Additional vertebral body metastases at T3, T9, L1, L4, and S1 with sacral involvement. A 4 cm paravertebral soft tissue mass at T7 extends into the left neural foramen. Urgent neurosurgical referral recommended."
- **Descriptor propagation:** Level of compression (changes surgical planning), degree of thecal sac compromise (partial vs near-complete vs complete — changes urgency), presence of cord myelopathy (changes urgency and prognosis), number and levels of additional metastases (changes staging and treatment planning). Descriptors that do NOT propagate: marrow signal characteristics, cortical breach pattern, enhancement pattern — these are diagnostic criteria for the named condition and remain in FINDINGS
- **Recommendation scope:**
  - REFERRAL: Urgent neurosurgical referral (same day) for assessment of decompression
  - REFERRAL: Urgent radiotherapy referral if not a surgical candidate
  - MDT: Spinal MDT or oncology MDT for treatment planning (not an acute step)
  - CORRELATION: Clinical correlation with neurological examination
  - Out of radiological scope: surgical technique, decompression level selection, radiotherapy dosing and field design, anticoagulation management, rehabilitation
- **Guideline hooks:** MSCC is a medical emergency per NICE guidance; the degree of compression (partial, near-complete, complete) and presence of cord signal change are the key imaging determinants of urgency; no specific RADS or scoring system applies to MSCC

# Skill Sheet: CT pancreas protocol (arterial and portal venous phases) — Staging for suspected pancreatic malignancy

## Scan Context
- **Modality:** Multiphasic CT pancreas protocol — arterial and portal venous phases, thin-section axial acquisition with coronal and sagittal reconstructions
- **Primary region:** Pancreas and peripancreatic structures
- **Imaged volume:** Dome of liver (at the diaphragm) to pelvic brim
- **In-scope:** Pancreas (head, body, tail), peripancreatic fat, duodenum, common bile duct, intrahepatic biliary tree, gallbladder, liver, portal vein and branches, superior mesenteric vein, superior mesenteric artery, celiac axis, hepatic artery, splenic artery, inferior vena cava, aorta, spleen, adrenals, kidneys, stomach, small bowel, colon, mesentery, omentum, retroperitoneal and mesenteric lymph nodes, peritoneum
- **Secondary visible regions:**
  - Lung bases → "The lung bases are clear."
  - Pelvic viscera → "The uterus and ovaries are unremarkable."
  - Vertebral column → "No osseous abnormality identified."
- **Out of scope:** Pancreatic duct microarchitecture and small intraductal lesions (requires MRCP or EUS); bone marrow metastatic infiltration (requires PET-CT or whole-body bone scan); cerebral metastases (requires CT head or MRI brain)
- **Contrast:** IV contrast, arterial and portal venous phases (as stated in scan-type name)
- **Modality non-assessables:** Pancreatic duct microarchitecture and intraductal lesions below approximately 3 mm not resolvable at standard CT resolution — requires MRCP or EUS; peritoneal deposits below approximately 5 mm unreliable on standard-resolution CT — requires diagnostic laparoscopy; trabecular bone marrow infiltration not assessable on CT — requires PET-CT or whole-body bone scan

## Clinical Lane
- **Question:** Stage suspected pancreatic malignancy — map the primary tumour extent, local vascular involvement, regional nodal disease, and distant metastases so the MDT can determine resectability and direct the treatment pathway
- **Purpose:** Staging
- **Primary hypothesis:** Pancreatic malignancy (pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma most likely given the clinical picture)
- **Differentials in scope:**
  - **Triage:** Pancreatic mass vs benign cause of pancreatic enlargement or ductal dilatation (autoimmune pancreatitis, chronic pancreatitis, neuroendocrine tumour, lymphoma, metastasis to pancreas)
  - **Aetiology (if pancreatic mass confirmed):**
    - Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma — hypovascular on arterial phase, ill-defined or infiltrative margins, main pancreatic duct obstruction with upstream dilatation, peripancreatic fat stranding, vascular encasement
    - Pancreatic neuroendocrine tumour — hypervascular arterial-phase enhancement, well-defined margins, less likely to cause upstream ductal dilatation
    - Autoimmune pancreatitis — diffuse or focal "sausage-shaped" enlargement, capsule-like rim, less discrete mass effect, less ductal obstruction
    - Chronic pancreatitis with inflammatory mass — pancreatic calcifications, irregular ductal dilatation, less discrete mass
    - Lymphoma — bulky homogeneous mass, less ductal dilatation, extensive nodal involvement
    - Metastasis to pancreas — well-defined, often multiple, typically with a known extra-pancreatic primary
  - **Aetiology (if no mass but ductal or biliary dilatation):**
    - Periampullary process too small to resolve as a discrete mass
    - Choledocholithiasis (less likely given the clinical context)
    - Intraductal stricture from a small pancreatic head lesion
  - **Imaging-silent aetiologies:**
    - Coagulopathy or bleeding risk *(imaging-silent — requires clinical/laboratory correlation)*
    - Nutritional status and cachexia *(imaging-silent — requires clinical correlation)*
- **Clinical history modifiers:**
  - Painless jaundice → localises the primary target to the pancreatic head and periampullary region; sweep leads with the pancreatic head and biliary tree; management implication: any head mass or periampullary process is the index finding and drives the entire report
  - 8 kg weight loss, bilirubin 180, CA 19-9 1200 → high pre-test probability of pancreatic malignancy; management implication: equivocal findings (small peripancreatic stranding, borderline lymph node, small hepatic lesion) should be flagged with high suspicion and carried into the impression; MDT referral is the default pathway regardless of whether a discrete mass is identified
  - 68F → establishes female gender for pelvic structures; management implication: pelvic sweep names the uterus and ovaries directly
  - Staging context → the entire study is directed at resectability assessment; management implication: vascular involvement of the superior mesenteric artery, superior mesenteric vein, portal vein, celiac axis, and hepatic artery is the critical finding and must be reported with degree of contact and length of involvement even if the primary mass is small

## Structural Pattern
- **Sections:** COMPARISON, TECHNIQUE, FINDINGS, IMPRESSION
- **P1 belongs:** Pancreatic mass (location, size, morphology, enhancement pattern), associated main pancreatic duct dilatation, common bile duct dilatation and level of obstruction, peripancreatic fat stranding or infiltration, vascular involvement (named vessel, degree, length), regional lymphadenopathy (station, size), peritoneal or omental deposits, hepatic metastases, adrenal metastases, lung base metastases, any other distant metastases within the imaged volume
- **P1 does NOT belong:** Unrelated incidental findings (simple renal cyst, degenerative vertebral change, unrelated bowel finding, small adrenal adenoma without metastatic morphology)
- **Primary system (priority-ordered):** Pancreatic mass first (location, size, morphology) → vascular involvement (named vessels, degree of contact, length) → ductal and biliary obstruction (level, calibre) → peripancreatic infiltration → regional lymphadenopathy → peritoneal and omental disease → distant metastases (liver, adrenals, lung bases) → residual anatomy
- **Sweep order:** Pancreas and peripancreatic structures (head, body, tail, peripancreatic fat, duodenum) → biliary tree (common bile duct, intrahepatic ducts, gallbladder) → liver → vascular structures (portal vein, superior mesenteric vein, superior mesenteric artery, celiac axis, hepatic artery, splenic artery, inferior vena cava, aorta) → spleen → adrenals → kidneys → stomach → small bowel → colon → mesentery and omentum → retroperitoneal and mesenteric nodes → peritoneum → lung bases → pelvis → bones and soft tissues
- **Macro-structure:** FLAT
- **Normal-study path:** The pancreas is normal in size and contour with no focal mass, no peripancreatic fat stranding, and no ductal dilatation. The common bile duct, intrahepatic biliary tree, and gallbladder are normal in calibre. The liver is normal in size, contour, and attenuation with no focal lesion. The portal vein, superior mesenteric vein, superior mesenteric artery, celiac axis, hepatic artery, splenic artery, inferior vena cava, and aorta are patent with no encasement, thrombosis, or aneurysm. The spleen, adrenals, and kidneys are normal in size and contour with no focal lesion. The stomach, small bowel, and colon are unremarkable with no wall thickening, obstruction, or mass. The mesentery and omentum are unremarkable. No retroperitoneal or mesenteric lymphadenopathy. No peritoneal or omental deposit. The lung bases are clear. The uterus and ovaries are unremarkable. No osseous or soft-tissue abnormality identified.

## Companion Matrix
- **In-scope companions:**
  - Pancreatic mass — location (head, body, tail), longest axis in mm, arterial-phase enhancement pattern (hypovascular vs hypervascular), margins (well-defined vs infiltrative), relationship to main pancreatic duct and common bile duct
  - Vascular involvement — named vessel, degree of contact (abutment <180° vs encasement ≥180° vs occlusion or thrombosis), length of contact in cm, luminal patency
  - Biliary obstruction — common bile duct calibre in mm at the level of obstruction, level (intrahepatic, common, distal), intrahepatic ductal dilatation (degree, distribution)
  - Main pancreatic duct dilatation — calibre in mm, level of obstruction, upstream distribution
  - Peripancreatic fat stranding or infiltration — extent (degrees of circumferential contact with the mass), degree (mild stranding vs dense infiltration)
  - Regional lymphadenopathy — station (peri-pancreatic, periduodenal, celiac, superior mesenteric, portal, para-aortic), short-axis diameter in mm, morphology (homogeneous vs necrotic, round vs oval)
  - Peritoneal or omental disease — location, size in mm, morphology (nodular deposits vs plaque-like omental caking)
  - Hepatic metastases — number, size in mm, segmental distribution, morphology (hypoattenuating, ring-enhancing, centripetal fill-in)
  - Adrenal metastases — side, size in mm, morphology (enlargement, irregular contour, hypoattenuating)
  - Duodenal or periampullary involvement — wall thickening, luminal narrowing, mass effect
- **Mandatory negatives:**
  - "No hypervascular arterial-phase enhancement to suggest pancreatic neuroendocrine tumour."
  - "No diffuse pancreatic enlargement with capsule-like rim to suggest autoimmune pancreatitis."
  - "No pancreatic calcifications or irregular ductal dilatation to suggest chronic pancreatitis."
  - "No peritoneal or omental deposit to suggest peritoneal carcinomatosis."
  - "No adrenal enlargement or focal lesion to suggest adrenal metastasis."
  - "No lung base nodule or consolidation to suggest pulmonary metastasis."
- **Out-of-scope suppressed:** Pancreatic duct microarchitecture and small intraductal lesions (requires MRCP or EUS); bone marrow metastatic infiltration (requires PET-CT or whole-body bone scan); cerebral metastases (requires CT head or MRI brain)

## Style Exemplars

- **Pancreatic mass (head)**
  - Abnormal (uncomplicated): "A 34 mm hypovascular mass is present in the head of the pancreas with ill-defined margins and extension into the peripancreatic fat. The main pancreatic duct is dilated to 8 mm proximal to the mass, and the common bile duct is dilated to 14 mm at the level of the pancreatic head."

- **Vascular involvement**
  - Abnormal (uncomplicated): "The mass abuts the superior mesenteric vein for 2.1 cm with luminal narrowing but no occlusion. The superior mesenteric artery, celiac axis, and hepatic artery are patent with no abutment or encasement."

- **Regional lymphadenopathy**
  - Abnormal (uncomplicated): "A 14 mm peripancreatic lymph node is identified medial to the pancreatic neck, homogeneous in attenuation. No other lymphadenopathy above 10 mm short-axis diameter is identified."

- **Hepatic metastases**
  - Abnormal (uncomplicated): "Two hypoattenuating hepatic lesions are identified, the largest 18 mm in segment V and a second 9 mm in segment VII, both with peripheral arterial-phase enhancement and centripetal fill-in on the portal venous phase."

## Terminology Rules
- **Preferred:** "hypovascular" (not "low-attenuation" or "hypodense" alone for a pancreatic mass on arterial phase — specifies the phase-dependent enhancement pattern that discriminates PDAC from PNET)
- **Preferred:** "encasement" (≥180° vascular contact) and "abutment" (<180° vascular contact) — do not use "invasion" or "involvement" generically; specify the degree of contact
- **Preferred:** "dilatation" (not "dilation" — British English)
- **Findings-only vs Impression-permitted:** "pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma" — the imaging features (hypovascular mass, ductal obstruction, peripancreatic infiltration) are described in FINDINGS; the diagnosis name is reserved for IMPRESSION synthesis
- **Findings-only vs Impression-permitted:** "resectable", "borderline resectable", "locally advanced" — these are MDT staging designations, not radiology report terms; the report describes the vascular relationship and the MDT assigns the category

## Conditional Suppression Rules
- IF the pancreatic mass is named with its vascular relationships in P1, the sweep paragraph for the pancreas names the structure only without restating the mass descriptor or vascular contacts.
- IF no vascular involvement is identified, state it as a single compact negative in FINDINGS: "No vascular encasement or occlusion of the superior mesenteric artery, superior mesenteric vein, portal vein, celiac axis, or hepatic artery." Carry into the IMPRESSION as a direct negative answer. Do not elaborate in both locations.
- IF no lymphadenopathy is identified, render one line: "No retroperitoneal or mesenteric lymphadenopathy." Do not enumerate each station individually.
- IF multiple negatives fire in one subsystem (e.g. no peritoneal deposit, no omental disease, no mesenteric nodal enlargement), consolidate into a single sentence.
- IF dictation is silent about an in-scope structure the sweep visits, render the structure's canonical default-normal line at its sweep position. If a dictated positive implicates the structure as a companion (e.g. a pancreatic mass with peripancreatic infiltration), the canonical normal line for the peripancreatic fat is dropped or rendered in contingent form.
- IF a descriptor is mentioned once in P1, it is not repeated in subsequent sweep paragraphs; structures are described in one place.
- IF adjacent-in-sweep structures are all normal, consolidate into a single paragraph. A paragraph earns its own boundary only when it carries a positive finding, a differential-targeted negative, or a clinical pivot between body regions.
- IF the clinical history establishes female gender (68F), pelvic canonical lines name the uterus and ovaries directly.

## Measurement Conventions
- **Pancreatic mass:** Longest axis in mm, location (head, body, tail) — required for all masses; arterial-phase enhancement pattern (hypovascular vs hypervascular) stated qualitatively
- **Vascular involvement:** Degree of contact (abutment <180° / encasement ≥180° / occlusion), length of contact in cm — required for every named vessel in contact with the mass; luminal patency stated
- **Biliary and ductal dilatation:** Common bile duct calibre in mm at the level of obstruction, main pancreatic duct calibre in mm — required when dilatation is present; level of obstruction stated

## Impression Exemplars

- **Opening convention:** Index finding (pancreatic mass) when confirmed; if no mass but ductal or biliary dilatation is present, the ductal finding opens. A negative study leads with the negative answer to the staging question.
- **Normal exemplar:** "No pancreatic mass, ductal dilatation, or biliary obstruction identified. No vascular encasement or occlusion of the superior mesenteric artery, superior mesenteric vein, portal vein, celiac axis, or hepatic artery. No regional lymphadenopathy or distant metastatic disease. No peritoneal or omental deposit. No adrenal abnormality."
- **Abnormal exemplar:** "Mass in the head of the pancreas with main pancreatic duct and common bile duct obstruction. Superior mesenteric vein abutment 2.1 cm with luminal narrowing; no superior mesenteric artery or celiac axis involvement. A 14 mm peripancreatic lymph node is present. Two small hepatic lesions are suspicious for metastatic disease. Findings are most consistent with pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma. Pancreatic MDT review recommended."
- **Complicated exemplar:** "Mass in the body of the pancreas with superior mesenteric artery encasement and splenic vein occlusion. Multiple peritoneal deposits and omental caking. Diffuse hepatic metastatic disease. Bilateral adrenal enlargement consistent with metastatic disease. Findings are most consistent with metastatic pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma. Pancreatic MDT review recommended."
- **Descriptor propagation:** Vascular contact degree and length (determines resectability pathway), lymph node size above 10 mm (N staging), presence of hepatic or peritoneal metastases (M staging), splenic vein or portal vein occlusion (portal hypertension risk, surgical planning) propagate into the impression. Mass size, enhancement pattern, margin character, and ductal calibre are diagnostic-criterion descriptors that stay in FINDINGS — the diagnosis name encodes them.
- **Recommendation scope:**
  - MDT: Pancreatic MDT review (named UK multidisciplinary team for pancreatic malignancy)
  - IMAGING: MRCP if biliary tree detail is required to delineate the level of obstruction for MDT planning
  - TISSUE: EUS-guided fine-needle aspiration or biopsy for histological diagnosis where imaging is equivocal or tissue is required before MDT
  - CORRELATION: Clinical and laboratory correlation (liver function tests, CA 19-9 trend)
- **Guideline hooks:** NICE NG12 (Pancreatic cancer: diagnosis and management); resectability criteria based on vascular involvement (NCCN/ESMO criteria as adapted in UK practice) — the report describes the vascular relationship; the MDT assigns the resectability category
